# Results — Study 34 (Aftershock): post-earnings-announcement drift (PEAD) on the real tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The book is a **dollar-neutral
long-positive / short-negative-SUE PEAD book** on the cross-section of S&P 500 names: at each earnings
announcement, weight each name by its standardised unexpected earnings (SUE), hold ~60 trading days,
dollar-neutral across the live cross-section, entry **lagged one day** after the filing (strictly causal).
The SUE is a **seasonal random walk** — ``surprise_q = eps_q − eps_{q−4}`` (year-over-year EPS change, the
classic Bernard-Thomas measure that needs no analyst estimate), standardised by the stock's own **trailing**
surprise dispersion. The announcement date is the **earliest `filed` date** per quarter from cached EDGAR
EPS; the price panel is the cached S&P 500 split/dividend-adjusted closes. As-of **2026-06-05**; match the
fingerprint below. **Caveat:** the panel is today's index membership → survivorship bias; the qualitative
result (a small, real drift whose break-even sits inside realistic costs) is robust, exact magnitudes are
biased upward by the missing delisted losers.*

## The verdict, earned — Signal `WEAK` · Tradability `MIRAGE` · Drift decays as predicted? `CONFIRMED`

Post-earnings-announcement drift is one of the most **robustly documented anomalies in finance** (Ball-Brown
1968; Bernard-Thomas 1989, 1990), and on the real tape it shows up — but *thin*. The dollar-neutral
long-high-SUE / short-low-SUE book earns a gross Sharpe of just **+0.30** (CAGR +0.8%, vol 3.0%) over
2010–2026, with a **Newey-West *t*-stat of +1.39** (plain *t* +1.21) — i.e. the drift is present and points
the right way, but it is **not statistically distinguishable from zero at conventional levels** on this
sample. So the signal is real-but-`WEAK`, not the resounding `REAL` the literature's *gross* effect would
suggest — exactly what fifty years of attenuation (McLean & Pontiff 2016) and a liquid large-cap universe
predict. The **drift-decay curve `CONFIRMED`** the under-reaction shape it is famous for: the surprise-signed
cumulative abnormal return rises monotonically from **+0.14% (day 0) to +1.15% (day 69)**, Bernard-Thomas's
Figure 1 reproduced on real earnings. But tradability is a textbook **`MIRAGE`**: the book turns over slowly
(**0.058/day**, paced by the earnings calendar), yet the gross edge is so small that its **break-even cost is
only 6.0 bp** — *inside* the realistic equity round-trip band (≈2–10 bp once you add spread and impact), and
that 6 bp is itself **inflated by survivorship** (the missing delisted losers would only lower it). Net of a
gentle 5 bp the Sharpe is already **+0.05** (≈ nothing); net of 10 bp it is **−0.20**.

## Data stamp

- **Earnings**: cached EDGAR quarterly EPS, deduped to earliest-filed announcements → SUE (seasonal random
  walk, trailing-standardised). **23,000 announcement events**, **488 names**, 2010–2026.
- **Panel**: cached S&P 500 split/dividend-adjusted closes → returns, 2010-01-04 → 2026-06-05, 4,131 days,
  inputs fingerprint `83140e2fef71`, as-of `2026-06-05`.
- **Caveat**: current-membership panel ⇒ survivorship bias (delisted names absent); SUE = seasonal random
  walk (no analyst estimate), so it is the *standardised* surprise, not an estimate-relative miss.

## The PEAD book — real gross, gone net

| | Sharpe | CAGR | vol | max-DD | skew |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PEAD (gross, 0 bp)** | **+0.30** | +0.8% | 3.0% | −6% | −0.64 |
| PEAD (net @5 bp) | +0.05 | +0.1% | 3.0% | −8% | −0.64 |
| PEAD (net @10 bp) | −0.20 | −0.6% | 3.0% | −14% | −0.65 |

Gross mean **Newey-West *t*-stat +1.39** (plain +1.21). A positive, correctly-signed gross drift — but
small, marginally significant, and erased by any realistic cost.

## The cost wall — a 6 bp break-even

| cost (bp/unit) | 0 | 2 | 5 | 10 | 20 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| net Sharpe | +0.298 | +0.199 | +0.050 | −0.199 | −0.691 |

Turnover is **0.058/day**, so the **break-even cost is 6.0 bp**. That sits *inside* the realistic
round-trip cost band for S&P names — and survivorship bias makes the true break-even lower still. The slow
roll (the earnings calendar, not a daily reshuffle) is the book's one advantage, and it is not enough.
`MIRAGE`.

## The horizon — you must hold the full quarter

Holding-period sweep (gross / net @5 bp Sharpe, turnover/day):

| hold (days) | 5 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 90 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| gross Sharpe | +0.272 | +0.209 | +0.265 | **+0.298** | +0.189 |
| net @5 bp | −0.659 | −0.342 | −0.187 | **+0.050** | +0.038 |
| turnover/day | 0.513 | 0.194 | 0.113 | 0.058 | 0.035 |

Short holds pay all the turnover and miss the slow drift (net −0.66 at 5 days); only at a ~60-day hold does
the cumulative drift catch up to the costs — and even then it merely reaches break-even. The drift is real
but *slow*: you must hold the full quarter to bank it, exactly as the decay curve says.

## The aftershock itself — the drift-decay curve `CONFIRMED`

Mean surprise-signed cumulative abnormal return by trading-day since the announcement (window 70):

| day | 0 | 5 | 10 | 20 | 30 | 40 | 50 | 60 | 69 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| signed CAR | +0.0014 | +0.0025 | +0.0030 | +0.0032 | +0.0037 | +0.0059 | +0.0076 | +0.0096 | +0.0115 |

The curve rises monotonically over the post-event quarter — the Bernard-Thomas (1989) under-reaction
signature, reproduced on real earnings. That *shape* is the anomaly, and it is what makes the book hold for
weeks (and therefore turn over slowly). The drift is genuinely there; it is just too small, on the liquid
large-cap names you can actually trade, to clear costs.
